item.title: Links of minimum degree and exact covering numbers
item.description: arXiv:2610.31696v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The covering number $C(v,k,t)$ is the least number of $k$-subsets, called blocks, of a $v$-set such that every $t$-subset lies in one of them. We reduce the question whether a covering with $L$ blocks exists to the classification of links. If every point of such a covering lies in at least $r$ blocks and $(r+1)v>kL$, some point lies in exactly $r$ blocks, and its link, the blocks through it with the point removed, is a $(v-1,k-1,t-1)$-covering with $r$ blocks. It then suffices to list these links up to isomorphism, to prove the list complete, and to show that no link in the list extends to a covering with $L$ blocks. Completeness is certified by one unsatisfiable formula that excludes the listed classes, so the program that lists the links need not be trusted. In general the last two steps are decided by propositional satisfiability (SAT) solving, with every formula written by two separately implemented encoders and every refutation checked by a formally verified proof checker. For links with four blocks and $t=3$ we give the classification by hand, under a condition on the parameters. As an application we determine twenty-five covering numbers with $t\in\{3,4,5\}$ in which the published lower bound was one less than the size of a known covering, among them $C(39,24,3)=9$.
item.dc:creator: Alfonso Gippini Requeijo

item.title: The Minimum Number of Samples in the Labeled Coupon Collector Problem
item.description: arXiv:2610.32251v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Labeled Coupon Collector Problem (LCCP) is an extension of the classical Coupon Collector Problem (CCP) in which one must deduce an unknown mapping between coupons and labels by collecting unordered subsets of k coupons and their associated labels, where deduction relies on analyzing the intersections and differences of the unordered subsets. In this work, we establish a fundamental connection between the LCCP and the combinatorial theory of separating systems. Using this framework, we completely characterize the minimum required number of samples to deduce all labels in two settings: Type-I, where the label set is known in advance, and Type-II, where it is unknown. We provide deterministic constructions of minimal separating and covering systems, yielding explicit bounds that are tighter than those found in existing literature. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to the partial recovery problem, characterizing the minimum number of samples required to identify a specified number of target coupons.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Tan, Daniella Bar-Lev, Ryan Gabrys, Zohar Yakhini, Paul H. Siegel

item.title: Stable Set Reconfiguration in Dense Digraphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.32402v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In a directed graph, a stable (or acyclic) set is a set which does not induce a directed cycle. Given a directed graph and two acyclic sets of the same size, the Acyclic-Set-Reconfiguration with Directed Token Sliding (ASR) problem asks whether one can, by iteratively replacing a vertex by an adjacent one, transform the first set into the second one, while maintaining acyclicity during the transformation. In this work, we present a study of the complexity of ASR and provide an FPT algorithm for semi-complete digraphs, when parametrized by the size of the sets being reconfigured, the directed pathwidth (or equivalently, the directed treewidth) of the instance, and a newly introduced parameter called the iteration of the reconfiguration sequence. To the best of our knowledge, the reconfiguration of stable sets has only been studied on undirected graphs, or (more recently) on sparse directed graphs.
item.dc:creator: Sarah Houdaigoui, Nacim Oijid, Matthieu Petiteau, Alexandre Vigny

item.title: Identifying codes of Archimedean grids
item.description: arXiv:2610.32192v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: An identifying code of a graph is a dominating set $C$ such that the sets $N[v]\cap C$ are pairwise distinct. The minimum density of an identifying code has been studied extensively for several infinite grids. It is known to be $1/4$ for the triangular grid and $7/20$ for the square grid, whereas for the hexagonal grid the problem is still open, between $5/12$ and $53/126$. These three grids are the regular members of the family of the eleven Archimedean grids. In this paper, we start a systematic study of identifying codes in this family. We determine the minimum density for five of the nine Archimedean grids for which it was not known: it is $2/3$ for the truncated hexagonal grid $3.12.12$, $3/7$ for the truncated square grid $4.8.8$, and $1/3$ for the trihexagonal (kagome) grid $3.6.3.6$, the elongated triangular grid $3^3.4^2$ and the snub hexagonal grid $3^4.6$. All lower bounds are proved by the discharging method. For the three remaining non-regular Archimedean grids, we also obtain some bounds: the minimum density lies between $3/7$ and $13/30$ for the truncated trihexagonal grid $4.6.12$, between $1/3$ and $11/30$ for the rhombitrihexagonal grid $3.4.6.4$, and between $2/7$ and $9/28$ for the snub square grid $3^2.4.3.4$.
item.dc:creator: Rudini Sampaio

item.title: Eternal Vertex Cover Problem on Halin Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2607.23155v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Eternal vertex cover problem is a graph protection problem which is a dynamic two player game variant of the classical vertex cover problem. In this game, the minimum number of guards required to protect a graph $G$ is called the eternal vertex cover number of $G$, denoted by $evc(G)$. It is known that for any graph $G$, $\ mvc(G) \le evc(G) \le 2mvc(G)$, where $mvc(G)$ is the vertex cover number of $G$, and that these bounds are generally tight. However, no biconnected graph $G$ achieves $evc(G) = 2mvc(G)$ and no better lower bounds are known for them. In this work, we focus on biconnected graphs in graph families. For infinite graph families $\mathcal{F}$, consider the parameter $\rho(\mathcal{F})=\sup\{r \in \mathbb{R}:\text{ for infinitely many graphs }G \in \mathcal{F},\frac{evc(G)}{mvc(G)}\ge r\}$. No class of biconnected graphs $\mathcal{F}$ is known yet, for which $1 < \rho(\mathcal{F})<2$. In this paper, we show that when $\mathcal{F}$ is the family of Halin graphs, $\frac{7}{6} \le \rho(\mathcal{F}) \le \frac{3}{2}$. Halin graphs are $3$-connected and they have treewidth three. To show the lower bound, we construct a family of Halin graphs for which the ratio tends to $\frac{7}{6}$ with increasing graph size. For the upper bound, we give two algorithms. Our first algorithm gives a defense strategy with $\frac{3}{2} mvc(G)$ guards and serves as a $\frac{3}{2}$ factor approximation algorithm to compute the eternal vertex cover number of Halin graphs. This algorithm also gives an upper bound of $\frac{4}{3}$ for $\rho$ for several subclasses of Halin graphs. Our second algorithm attains the upper bound of $\frac{4}{3}$ for caterpillar Halin graphs. Whether computing eternal vertex cover number is NP-hard for Halin graphs remains an open problem, as is the case with treewidth two graphs.
item.dc:creator: Jasine Babu, Pratik Ghosal, Cipriyano Simoes

item.title: Tournaments determined by three and five voters
item.description: arXiv:2607.26690v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pairwise majority has been studied since Ramon Llull in the 13th century and Condorcet in the 18th. A tournament records, for each pair of alternatives, which one a majority of voters prefers. A committee of $m$ voters produces only some tournaments; let $N(m)$ be the smallest number of alternatives on which some tournament cannot arise from any $m$ voters. Only $N(3) = 8$ is known. We refute three conjectures. Every minimum feedback arc set of a tournament is a minimal set of arcs meeting every cyclic triangle, strengthening a theorem of Milosz, Hamel and Pierrot on Kemeny medians of three voters, and both of their conjectures fail. The third, going back to a question of Shepardson and Tovey, is that $m$ voters produce every tournament of predictability at least $(m+1)/(2m)$, predictability being the largest $\alpha$ for which some electorate produces the tournament with every majority backed by a fraction $\alpha$ of the voters. It fails for three voters: up to isomorphism, exactly 1,013 tournaments on ten alternatives have predictability $2/3$ yet arise from no three voters, none on fewer alternatives does, and failures occur only at the threshold. For five voters we show $12 \le N(5) \le 38$ and give the first explicit tournament of moderate size that no five voters produce, the Paley tournament on 43 alternatives; its predictability exceeds $3/5$, so the conjecture fails even strictly above the threshold. A companion paper narrows the bounds to $13 \le N(5) \le 22$. Public code reproduces every computation.
item.dc:creator: Leonid Chindelevitch, Ararat Harutyunyan

item.title: Tournaments not inducible by five voters
item.description: arXiv:2609.13924v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: How many members must a committee have before its pairwise majorities can express any collective preference? With enough voters every pattern of pairwise majorities, or tournament, can arise, but a committee of $k$ voters produces only some; for odd $k$, let $N(k)$ be the least number of alternatives on which some tournament arises from no $k$ voters. Only $N(3) = 8$ is known; for five voters our companion paper gave $12 \le N(5) \le 38$ and the first explicit example of moderate size, on 43 vertices. We show $13 \le N(5) \le 22$. The upper bound comes from nine tournaments on 22 vertices that five voters cannot produce: eight one-vertex deletions of doubly regular tournaments on 23 vertices, including every deletion of one of them, and one arc reversal. The Paley tournament on 23 vertices, which Bachmeier et al. (2019) left open after six weeks of SAT solving, is beyond five voters, and so is every other doubly regular tournament on 23 vertices. The lower bound comes from an analysis of all tournaments on 12 vertices. Both doubly regular tournaments on 19 vertices, the Paley tournament and one other, arise from five voters, but not with unit margin, that is, not with every majority carried by three votes to two. The method is a search that places one alternative at a time and exploits the tournament's symmetries; four of the negative results are certified by machine-checkable proofs, and all results are reproducible from a public repository.
item.dc:creator: Leonid Chindelevitch, Ararat Harutyunyan

item.title: Computing distances in braid-move graphs, higher Bruhat orders, and oriented-matroid mutation graphs is NP-hard
item.description: arXiv:2610.03808v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A wiring diagram is an arrangement of $m$ pseudolines, every two of which cross exactly once. Reading its crossings from left to right encodes it as a reduced word of the permutation $w_0\in S_m$ that reverses $1,\dots,m$, unique up to commutations, and a braid move $\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i\leftrightarrow\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}$ flips one of its triangles. We prove that deciding whether two wiring diagrams are within a given braid-move distance is NP-complete. Equivalently, deciding flip distance is NP-complete in the higher Bruhat order $B(m,2)$, for triangle flips of marked arrangements of pseudolines, and for rhombic tilings of a $2m$-gon; this answers an open question on flip graphs of pseudoline arrangements (SODA 2024). The reduction is from Vertex Cover: for every graph $G$ we construct two wiring diagrams at braid-move distance $|D|+2\operatorname{VC}(G)$, where $\operatorname{VC}(G)$ is the vertex cover number of $G$ and the Hamming distance $|D|$ is the number of triples of wires whose triangles are oriented differently. The construction glues copies of a seven-wire gadget whose braid-move distance exceeds its Hamming distance by $2$. Adding a line at infinity transfers the construction to rank-$3$ uniform oriented matroids, where two oriented matroids are adjacent in the mutation graph if their chirotopes differ in one basis; so deciding distance in the mutation graph is NP-complete in rank $3$. An iterate of Rambau's expansion of signotopes amplifies the excess and gives NP-hardness in every fixed rank $r\ge4$, and by duality in every fixed corank at least $3$. The same instances show that flip distance in the higher Bruhat orders $B(n,k)$ is NP-complete for every fixed $k\ge2$.
item.dc:creator: Tilen Marc

item.title: Multi-Capacity Online Assortment Optimization with Consecutive Stays under Markov Chain Choice
item.description: arXiv:2610.27661v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study online assortment optimization under Markov chain choice and independent Bernoulli arrivals, with each period's request type known in advance. Each product may have multiple interchangeable physical copies, and each booking reserves consecutive service slots on a single copy. Customers choose among products, while the platform assigns purchases to feasible copies. We develop a sales-based relaxation that upper-bounds the optimal online revenue and use it to design a policy with two components: independent sampling and purchase--update coupling. We generate independent copy proposals and make a product eligible whenever at least one of its copies proposes. A general revenue-extraction bound for random candidate sets with independent product inclusions shows that optimizing over eligible products recovers at least half of each period's relaxation revenue benchmark in expectation. A purchase--update coupling reproduces the interval flows through independent virtual copy updates while preserving physical feasibility. Under general Markov chain choice, the policy uses a random gate to make the coupling feasible: it offers the selected assortment with probability \(1-1/e\) and the empty assortment otherwise. No gate is needed under multinomial logit (MNL) choice. The resulting policies achieve approximation ratios of \((1-1/e)/2\) and \(1/2\), respectively, relative to the optimal nonanticipative online policy, independently of product capacities. In the single-copy MNL setting, our policy improves the guarantee of \citet{huwu2026} from \(0.271\) to \(1/2\) under the same arrival convention. The \(1/2\) static extraction factor and the \(1-1/e\) uniform scalar-gate factor are separately sharp, and the \(1/2\) MNL guarantee is tight for the proposed policy.
item.dc:creator: Hongbin Zhang, Yanzhi Li, Woonghee Tim Huh

item.title: The Size of the Intersection of $q$-ary Hamming Balls
item.description: arXiv:2606.09158v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The interest in studying the size of the intersection of multiple $q$-ary Hamming balls has grown due to the recent advances in DNA-based data storage systems. We present an exact formula for the cardinality of the intersection of $s$ Hamming balls of varying radii over a $q$-ary alphabet. It is known that the distances between the center points of the Hamming balls are not enough, in general, to determine the size of the intersection. Based on our formula, we are able to find more refined structural properties of the center points for determining the exact size of the intersection. Moreover, we also analyze the size of the intersection of Hamming balls with equal radii $t$ for sufficiently large $n$ when $t$ and $q$ are constants. When $s=3$, we give the necessary and sufficient conditions (for all $q\ge 2$, $q\neq 6$ and sufficiently large $n$) to obtain the maximum size of the intersection when the centers of the Hamming balls have a given minimum distance and demonstrate how to compute it using our general formula.
item.dc:creator: Ville Junnila, Tero Laihonen, Tuomo Lehtil\"a, Pavan Padavu Devaraj

item.title: Broadcast Domination Number is at Most Twice the Multipacking Number
item.description: arXiv:2608.20036v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: For a graph $ G = (V, E) $ with a vertex set $ V $ and an edge set $ E $, a function $ f : V \rightarrow \{0, 1, 2, . . . , diam(G)\} $ is called a \emph{broadcast} on $ G $. For each vertex $ u \in V $, if there exists a vertex $ v $ in $ G $ (possibly, $ u = v $) such that $ f (v) > 0 $ and $ d(u, v) \leq f (v) $, then $ f $ is called a dominating broadcast on $ G $. The cost of the dominating broadcast $f$ is the quantity $ \sum_{v\in V}f(v) $. The minimum cost of a dominating broadcast is the broadcast domination number of $G$, denoted by $ \gamma_{b}(G) $. A multipacking is a set $ M \subseteq V $ in a graph $ G = (V, E) $ such that for every vertex $ v \in V $ and for every integer $ r \geq 1 $, the ball of radius $ r $ around $ v $ contains at most $ r $ vertices of $ M $, that is, there are at most $ r $ vertices in $ M $ at a distance at most $ r $ from $ v $ in $ G $. The multipacking number of $ G $ is the maximum cardinality of a multipacking of $ G $ and is denoted by $ mp(G) $. It is known that $mp(G)\leq\gamma_b(G)$. In 2014, Hartnell and Mynhardt proved that $\gamma_b(G)\leq 3mp(G)-2$ whenever $mp(G)\geq2$. In 2019, Beaudou, Brewster, and Foucaud improved this bound to $\gamma_b(G)\leq 2 mp(G)+3$ and conjectured that $\gamma_b(G)\leq 2 mp(G)$. We solve their conjecture by proving that $\gamma_b(G)\leq 2 mp(G)$ for every graph $G$. Our proof is constructive and yields a linear-time $2$-approximation algorithm for Maximum Multipacking problem which improves the earlier approximation factor $2+o(1)$.
item.dc:creator: Sk Samim Islam
